title: 2666: The Part About the Critics
summary: Bolaño writes like the villain. He never tells you what's worth focus, but will make you feel dumb for asking.
body:
2666's first part is like drinking from an expensive fire hose. I can't get everything, but the little I get paints a rich atmosphere.

There's no effort made to identify the important. The story isn't shaved down for my consumption. Entire episodes seem to exist without any influence on the narrative, like they really happened and the book just documents it. It's overwhelming and tedious, but convincing.

The critics are goobers. They're self-important people living unremarkable lives. We're supposed to identify with them and be irritated by their mediocrity at the same time. Their obsession with Archimboldi is them trying to give their boring lives meaning by their association. The joke I read from it all is that the reader is just another critic, as desperate as they are for the story to mean something. We too want to find Archimboldi, because maybe then everything will come into focus.

The obscure literary references don't need to be understood. (At least, I didn't understand all of them.) I think it's enough to just know someone obscure is being referenced. They don't need to communicate any information, but they certainly establish this is a world that doesn't owe the reader an explanation. It's meta, but HOW meta is never made clear, and trying to figure that out feels suspiciously like falling into the same trap as the critics.

Bolaño writes like the villain. He never tells you what's worth focus, but will make you feel dumb for asking. I can't decide whether the book is extraordinarily profound or just very good at making me suspect that it is. That's probably what he wanted it to be.
creator: Roberto Bolaño

title: products are promises
summary: How software transformed companies from sellers of products into architects of the future.
body:
Technology has become the infrastructure of nearly every industry, and companies are increasingly selling something more ambitious than products: participation in a future of their own design.

In this Paper Antenna essay, I examine how technology companies construct narratives around the problems they're promising to solve.

title: A Little Mind: Giving Language Model Parameters a Face
summary: I built a small, slightly strange instrument for playing with the statistical controls behind language models. It's a design experiment in making abstract systems feel understandable.
body:
I've been experimenting with local language models lately, and something about their controls has always seemed funny to me. Temperature, Top-P, Top-K, repetition penalties: a handful of little numbers can completely change how a model behaves, but they're presented as if their meaning is self-evident.

They're not really human qualities, either. A model might seem more exploratory or more rigid when you adjust them, but there isn't a clean psychological equivalent for any of these statistical mechanisms. I wanted to design around that disconnect rather than explain it away.

So I built A Little Mind. It's a compact sampling instrument with a tiny illustrated face at its center. When you turn a dial or drag a probability control, the face reacts. Let go, and it settles right back into its vacant little blinking routine. The surrounding graphics give each parameter its own visual logic, while the numeric readouts keep the instrument useful.

The public version is an interactive React prototype. Its probability distribution and generated words are simulated, explicitly, so you can play with the concepts without needing a model running. Connecting it reliably to LM Studio and other local backends is the next engineering step, along with figuring out how to package it as a proper add-on.

I like building interfaces that make complicated systems a little less opaque. This one also gets to have a face.

title: Blog Publisher Gets Smarter
summary: I just finished a small but useful upgrade to the blog publisher behind emitrice.com. The publisher now has a post history view, so I can see previously published posts and delete old ones directly from the tool. More importantly, email upd
body:
I just finished a small but useful upgrade to the blog publisher behind emitrice.com.

The publisher now has a post history view, so I can see previously published posts and delete old ones directly from the tool. More importantly, email updates are now optional per post.
When I publish something, I can choose whether it should also send an email to subscribers. Bigger updates can still hit the inbox, while smaller notes, experiments, and quick progress posts can stay quietly on the site.

The whole flow now connects the publisher, GitHub, Render, and Resend into one cleaner system, with clearer feedback about whether a post was published and whether an email was actually sent.
